heading: Jesus knows His churches.
time: These messages first address four real churches in Asia Minor. Their promises also look ahead to resurrection and Christ’s kingdom.

scenes.title: Ephesus: return to your first love
scenes.text: Jesus values patient faithfulness but warns that love has been abandoned. Remembering, repenting and returning to the first works belong together. Correct beliefs alone do not replace love.

scenes.title: Smyrna: faithful under pressure
scenes.text: This suffering church receives encouragement rather than a rebuke. Jesus knows its poverty and promises the crown of life. The hostility described here concerns particular opponents; it is not a judgment on Jewish people as a whole.

scenes.title: Pergamos: hold to the truth
scenes.text: Some believers remain loyal even under deadly pressure, while others accept teaching that leads to idolatry and immorality. Jesus calls the church to repent instead of making peace with destructive compromise.

scenes.title: Thyatira: love with discernment
scenes.text: Jesus recognises growing service and endurance but confronts a corrupting teacher called Jezebel. He searches hearts and calls the faithful to hold fast until He comes.

symbols.title: Tree of life
symbols.text: The promise points back to Eden and forward to restored life with God.

symbols.title: Jezebel
symbols.text: The name recalls a queen who promoted false worship. Here it describes a corrupting influence within a church; the text does not invite us to label women generally this way.

symbols.title: Morning star
symbols.text: Jesus promises the morning star to the overcomer, and later calls Himself the bright morning star.

connections.title: Food offered to idols
connections.text: Paul also discusses idolatry and loyalty to Christ. Read the whole argument rather than treating every shared meal as false worship.

connections.title: God examines the heart
connections.text: Jeremiah’s language helps explain Jesus’ claim to know motives as well as actions.

questions.question: Does Jesus notice quiet service?
questions.answer: Yes. He names love, service, faith and patience in Thyatira even while correcting its failures.

questions.question: What does Ephesus need to recover?
questions.answer: Its first love, expressed through repentance and renewed action.

questions.question: What is promised to faithful Smyrna?
questions.answer: The crown of life and freedom from the second death.

interpretation.title: A message across history
interpretation.text: Historicist readers also see the churches as a picture of successive experiences in church history. That is an additional interpretation: these verses themselves address named communities and give no dated timetable of church eras.

reflection: Where does your faith need both deeper love and greater courage?
prayer: Jesus, restore my love and help me remain faithful under pressure. Amen.

heading: Hear the One knocking.
time: The last three letters address real churches. Their calls to wakefulness also prepare readers for Christ’s future coming.

scenes.title: Sardis: wake up
scenes.text: A good reputation can hide spiritual weakness. Jesus tells the church to remember what it received, hold fast and repent. A few have remained faithful, and their faithfulness is recognised.

scenes.title: Philadelphia: keep holding on
scenes.text: Jesus sets an open door before a church with little strength. He knows its loyalty and promises a lasting place with God. Their security rests in His authority, not their influence.

scenes.title: Laodicea: receive what you lack
scenes.text: The church thinks it is rich but does not recognise its need. Jesus offers true riches, clothing and sight. His rebuke comes with love and an invitation to fellowship.

symbols.title: Key of David
symbols.text: Isaiah pictures a key as authority to open and shut. Revelation applies this language to Jesus.

symbols.title: White clothing
symbols.text: Clothing pictures the opposite of shame and defilement. Other visions associate white robes with those cleansed through the Lamb.

symbols.title: Gold and eye medicine
symbols.text: The images expose false self-sufficiency. Christ supplies enduring spiritual riches and the ability to recognise our real condition.

connections.title: A welcome at the door
connections.text: The meal in verse 20 pictures fellowship. Jesus’ invitation follows a call to repentance, rather than ignoring the church’s condition.

connections.title: A secure place with God
connections.text: Isaiah promises an enduring name to those who belong to God. Philadelphia receives related language of belonging and permanence.

questions.question: Can a strong reputation hide a weak spiritual life?
questions.answer: Yes. Sardis has a name for being alive but is told to wake up.

questions.question: Does little strength mean Jesus has forgotten us?
questions.answer: No. Philadelphia has little strength, yet Jesus knows and encourages its faithfulness.

questions.question: Why does Jesus correct Laodicea?
questions.answer: He says that He rebukes and disciplines those He loves.

interpretation.title: Apply the warning personally
interpretation.text: In the historicist approach, Laodicea is especially associated with the church near the end. The useful response is self-examination, not declaring other people spiritually inferior. Every letter asks anyone with ears to listen.

reflection: What might change if you asked Jesus to show you a need you have overlooked?
prayer: Jesus, open my eyes and help me welcome Your correction and friendship. Amen.

heading: Look toward God’s throne.
time: The scene shifts from earthly churches to heavenly worship. The throne room provides the setting for the scroll and seals; it is not simply the next dated event on earth.

scenes.title: An open door into heaven
scenes.text: John is invited to see what must take place. A throne stands at the centre, with One seated upon it. Precious stones and a rainbow communicate splendour rather than an ordinary portrait of God.

scenes.title: Around the throne
scenes.text: John sees twenty-four elders, lamps, lightning and a sea like crystal. The carefully ordered scene contrasts with the uncertainty of earthly life.

scenes.title: Unceasing worship
scenes.text: Four living creatures praise God’s holiness. Their unusual appearance belongs to the vision’s symbolic language. Their song names the Lord as the One who was, is and is to come.

scenes.title: The Creator is worthy
scenes.text: The elders lay down their crowns and worship. Their reason is clear: God created all things. The chapter turns our attention from human power to the source of life.

symbols.title: Rainbow
symbols.text: Genesis connects the rainbow with God’s covenant. Around the throne it contributes to a picture of majesty framed by remembered mercy.

symbols.title: Four living creatures
symbols.text: Ezekiel also describes living creatures around divine glory. Similarities help us recognise throne-room imagery without assuming every detail is identical.

symbols.title: Seven lamps
symbols.text: Verse 5 calls them the seven Spirits of God. Understanding seven as fullness is an interpretation of the number, not seven separate gods.

connections.title: Holy, holy, holy
connections.text: Isaiah’s vision also centres on heavenly beings praising God’s holiness.

connections.title: Creation and worship
connections.text: The call to worship the Creator returns in the first angel’s message.

questions.question: Who is at the centre of the scene?
questions.answer: God upon His throne, surrounded by worship.

questions.question: Why is God declared worthy?
questions.answer: Because He created all things.

questions.question: What do the elders do with their crowns?
questions.answer: They cast them before the throne, acknowledging God’s worth.

interpretation.title: Begin with the heavenly setting
interpretation.text: A historicist reading follows the visions across history, but this scene first establishes who rules and deserves worship. It does not supply a date for each object around the throne. The identity of the twenty-four elders is not explicitly explained here.

reflection: How could remembering God as Creator change what you value today?
prayer: Creator God, teach me to honour You with gratitude and trust. Amen.

heading: The Lamb is worthy.
time: This continues the throne-room scene. The Lamb’s victory through death explains His worthiness before the seals begin to open.

scenes.title: A scroll no one can open
scenes.text: A sealed scroll lies in the right hand of the One on the throne. John weeps because no one is found worthy to open it or look into it.

scenes.title: The Lion appears as a Lamb
scenes.text: An elder announces the victorious Lion of Judah. John then sees a Lamb standing as though slain. Victory is revealed through the One who gave His life.

scenes.title: A new song
scenes.text: The elders and living creatures worship. Their song praises the Lamb’s redeeming death and describes a people drawn from every nation for God’s service.

scenes.title: All creation joins the praise
scenes.text: Countless angels proclaim the Lamb’s worth. The scene expands until every creature praises the One on the throne and the Lamb.

symbols.title: The slain Lamb
symbols.text: The Lamb represents Christ in the light of His sacrificial death. John’s Gospel also calls Jesus the Lamb of God.

symbols.title: Bowls of incense
symbols.text: The golden bowls contain incense, which the text identifies as the prayers of the saints.

symbols.title: Seven eyes
symbols.text: The eyes are identified as the seven Spirits of God sent into all the earth. The vision communicates divine activity beyond the throne room.

connections.title: The ruler from Judah
connections.text: The Lion of Judah recalls the royal promise associated with Judah.

connections.title: Suffering and victory
connections.text: Isaiah’s servant is compared with a lamb and bears others’ sins. This provides important background for the slain yet living Lamb.

questions.question: Why does John weep?
questions.answer: No one is found worthy to open the scroll.

questions.question: Why is the Lamb worthy?
questions.answer: He was slain and redeemed people for God by His blood.

questions.question: Whose prayers are represented by the incense?
questions.answer: The prayers of the saints, God’s people.

interpretation.title: Victory shapes the rest of the book
interpretation.text: Read the coming judgments in the light of this chapter: the worthy One is the Redeemer. Historicist interpretations of later events should remain centred on Christ, rather than making political predictions the main message.

reflection: How does Christ’s self-giving victory challenge your idea of power?
prayer: Jesus, thank You for redeeming us. Make my life a response to Your love. Amen.

heading: How long until justice comes?
time: The first six seals move through conquest, conflict and suffering toward the day of divine wrath. Historicist readers see a broad sweep of history; exact identifications are interpretive.

scenes.title: Four riders
scenes.text: A white horse is followed by red, black and pale horses. The visions show conquest, lost peace, scarcity and death. The text explicitly names the fourth rider Death; the identity of the first is debated.

scenes.title: The cry beneath the altar
scenes.text: Those slain for God’s word cry out for justice and receive white robes. This is a visionary picture of innocent blood calling for vindication, not a passage to isolate from the Bible’s wider teaching about death.

scenes.title: Creation shaken
scenes.text: The sixth seal brings an earthquake and startling changes in sun, moon, stars and sky. Familiar features of the world seem to give way.

scenes.title: Who can stand?
scenes.text: People of every rank seek shelter from the face of God and the wrath of the Lamb. The closing question leads directly into chapter 7.

symbols.title: Red horse
symbols.text: Its rider is permitted to take peace from the earth, so that people kill one another.

symbols.title: Balances and grain prices
symbols.text: Measured food at high cost suggests scarcity and hardship. The picture belongs to the third seal.

symbols.title: Blood crying for justice
symbols.text: Abel’s blood cries from the ground in Genesis. That image helps explain the appeal of the slain beneath the altar.

connections.title: Trouble before the end
connections.text: Jesus speaks of wars, famine and persecution while warning His followers against panic and deception.

connections.title: Who can endure?
connections.text: Malachi asks who can endure the Lord’s coming. Revelation answers its own similar question with a vision of God’s people.

questions.question: What does the fourth rider’s name tell us?
questions.answer: The pale horse is associated with death, followed by Hades, called hell in the KJV.

questions.question: What do the slain ask for?
questions.answer: God’s judgment and vindication, expressed as a cry for justice.

questions.question: What question closes the chapter?
questions.answer: Who will be able to stand before the great day of wrath?

interpretation.title: Distinguish the picture from a historical match
interpretation.text: Historicist readings associate the seals with developments across Christian history. The visions themselves should be studied before attaching dates or events to them. The text does not name a modern nation as any of the four riders.

reflection: How can you seek justice without giving up trust in God?
prayer: God of justice, sustain those who suffer and keep my hope in You. Amen.

heading: God knows those who are His.
time: This pause between the sixth and seventh seals answers the question of who can stand. It shows both protection before harm and a great multitude before God’s throne.

scenes.title: Hold back the winds
scenes.text: Four angels restrain destructive winds until God’s servants are sealed. The scene emphasises that God’s people are known to Him before the crisis unfolds.

scenes.title: The numbered servants
scenes.text: John hears the number 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. The list is deliberately arranged. Whether the number is literal or symbolic is a matter of interpretation.

scenes.title: A multitude from every nation
scenes.text: John sees an uncountable crowd in white robes, praising God and the Lamb. Salvation brings together people from every language and nation.

scenes.title: The Lamb becomes their Shepherd
scenes.text: The multitude has come through great tribulation. God shelters them; hunger, thirst and tears give way to the Lamb’s care.

symbols.title: Seal on the forehead
symbols.text: The seal marks God’s servants as belonging to Him. Later Revelation connects the forehead with the name of God and the Lamb.

symbols.title: White robes washed in blood
symbols.text: The elder says the robes are made white in the Lamb’s blood. Cleansing comes through His sacrifice, not the crowd’s own perfection.

symbols.title: Four winds
symbols.text: In this scene the restrained winds represent destructive forces held back. The instruction is to delay harm.

connections.title: A mark before judgment
connections.text: Ezekiel also describes a mark placed before a judgment scene. Compare the purpose without making every detail identical.

connections.title: A Shepherd and no more tears
connections.text: Isaiah promises guidance to water and the removal of tears. Revelation brings those hopes together around the Lamb.

questions.question: Who receives the seal?
questions.answer: The servants of God.

questions.question: Is the multitude limited to one nation?
questions.answer: No. It comes from all nations, peoples and languages.

questions.question: Who leads them to living water?
questions.answer: The Lamb, who shepherds them.

interpretation.title: Do not turn the number into a test of worth
interpretation.text: Adventist readers commonly relate the sealing to God’s faithful people in the final crisis. Christians differ about the 144,000 and their relationship to the great multitude. The chapter’s explicit hope is salvation through God and the Lamb.

reflection: How does belonging to God help you face uncertainty?
prayer: Loving Shepherd, guide me and help me welcome people from every nation. Amen.

heading: Prayer is heard as the trumpets sound.
time: The seventh seal opens, followed by a heavenly altar scene and four trumpets. This is a new vision sequence; readers should not assume every trumpet simply follows all the seals on a calendar.

scenes.title: Silence and prayer
scenes.text: Heaven is silent, and an angel presents incense with the prayers of the saints. Fire from the altar is then cast to earth. Prayer and judgment are held together in the scene.

scenes.title: The first trumpet
scenes.text: Hail and fire mixed with blood strike the earth. The imagery communicates a severe but limited judgment.

scenes.title: The second trumpet
scenes.text: Something like a burning mountain is cast into the sea. Sea life and ships suffer. John describes a comparison, not an identified modern weapon.

scenes.title: The third trumpet
scenes.text: A burning star called Wormwood falls upon waters, making them bitter. What normally sustains life becomes a source of suffering.

scenes.title: The fourth trumpet
scenes.text: Sun, moon and stars are darkened in part. A warning announces three further woes, preparing the reader for the remaining trumpets.

symbols.title: Incense and prayer
symbols.text: The incense is offered with the prayers of all the saints. Their cries are present before God.

symbols.title: Wormwood
symbols.text: The name evokes bitterness. Jeremiah also uses wormwood in descriptions of sorrow and judgment.

symbols.title: A third
symbols.text: The repeated fraction presents these judgments as limited. Chapter 16 later uses a more comprehensive pattern.

connections.title: Echoes of the Exodus
connections.text: Hail, blood and darkness recall the plagues on Egypt. These connections help us understand judgment and deliverance imagery.

connections.title: A burning mountain
connections.text: Jeremiah calls Babylon a destroying mountain that will become burnt. This is useful background rather than a complete explanation of the trumpet.

questions.question: Are the saints’ prayers forgotten?
questions.answer: No. They appear before God in the altar scene.

questions.question: What happens to the waters called Wormwood?
questions.answer: They become bitter, bringing death to many who drink.

questions.question: Have all seven trumpets sounded by this chapter’s end?
questions.answer: No. Four have sounded; three remain.

interpretation.title: Read carefully where interpreters differ
interpretation.text: Historicist readers understand the trumpets within the course of history, but Adventist scholars differ over particular identifications. This study first traces the biblical imagery instead of presenting one detailed timetable as explicit Scripture.

reflection: How can you keep praying when the world feels unstable?
prayer: Lord, hear our prayers and teach us to trust Your justice and mercy. Amen.

heading: Warnings call for a changed heart.
time: The fifth and sixth trumpets continue the sequence begun in chapter 8. Their frightening imagery ends by exposing humanity’s refusal to repent.

scenes.title: The fifth trumpet begins
scenes.text: A fallen star receives a key to the bottomless pit. Smoke darkens the air and locust-like creatures emerge. Their power is restricted, including a prohibition against harming those with God’s seal.

scenes.title: An extraordinary army
scenes.text: The creatures combine features of horses, people, lions and scorpions. Their king is named Destroyer. These are visionary descriptions; they should not be treated as a field guide to literal animals.

scenes.title: The sixth trumpet begins
scenes.text: Four bound angels are released at an appointed time. A vast mounted army enters the vision, and a third of humanity is killed.

scenes.title: The unanswered call to repentance
scenes.text: Fire, smoke and brimstone accompany the army. Yet survivors do not turn from idols, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality or theft. Outward crisis alone does not produce a changed heart.

symbols.title: Abaddon and Apollyon
symbols.text: These Hebrew and Greek names identify the king as Destroyer. The names stress destruction rather than providing a modern personal identity.

symbols.title: Scorpion-like tails
symbols.text: John connects them with the creatures’ ability to torment for five months.

symbols.title: Bottomless pit
symbols.text: Also translated abyss, this image suggests a realm of confinement and destructive activity. Its use varies with the surrounding scene.

connections.title: A locust invasion
connections.text: Joel’s army imagery gives important background to John’s descriptions of horses, teeth and overwhelming movement.

connections.title: Idols cannot save
connections.text: The closing verses echo biblical criticism of idols that cannot see, hear or walk.

questions.question: Is the torment without limits?
questions.answer: No. The vision specifies limits to whom the creatures may harm and for how long.

questions.question: What does the king’s name mean?
questions.answer: Destroyer.

questions.question: What do the survivors fail to do?
questions.answer: Repent of false worship and harmful actions.

interpretation.title: Avoid confident modern identifications
interpretation.text: Historicist interpretations of these trumpets have differed. The text names neither a modern military technology nor a current ethnic group. Its explicit closing concern is persistent false worship and unrepentant conduct.

reflection: What warning might you need to respond to with a practical change?
prayer: God, give me a teachable heart and courage to turn from what harms others. Amen.

heading: Receive the message, then share it.
time: This pause occurs between the sixth and seventh trumpets. John receives a renewed commission before the sequence resumes in chapter 11.

scenes.title: The mighty angel and the hidden words
scenes.text: An angel stands on sea and land with a little open book. Seven thunders speak, but John is told not to write their words. Revelation does not authorise us to invent that withheld message.

scenes.title: The promise will be completed
scenes.text: The angel swears by the Creator that God’s mystery will be finished in connection with the seventh trumpet. The KJV phrase about time is often understood as no further delay; its precise application is debated.

scenes.title: Sweet, then bitter
scenes.text: John eats the little book. It tastes sweet but becomes bitter in his stomach. He is then told to prophesy again to many peoples, nations, languages and kings.

symbols.title: Eating the book
symbols.text: Receiving a message is pictured as eating it. Ezekiel is also told to eat a scroll before speaking for God.

symbols.title: Sea and land
symbols.text: The angel’s stance suggests the wide reach of the message, matching the worldwide commission in verse 11.

symbols.title: Sweetness and bitterness
symbols.text: The contrasting experience suggests joy in receiving God’s word alongside the pain or difficulty involved in its fulfilment and proclamation.

connections.title: A sealed book and an oath
connections.text: Compare Daniel’s sealed words and the raised hand of the heavenly speaker with John’s open book and the angel’s oath.

connections.title: God’s word becomes joy
connections.text: Jeremiah describes receiving God’s words as eating them and finding joy in them.

questions.question: May John publish everything he hears?
questions.answer: No. The words of the seven thunders are sealed.

questions.question: What two experiences does the book bring?
questions.answer: Sweetness in his mouth and bitterness in his stomach.

questions.question: Does bitterness end John’s mission?
questions.answer: No. He must prophesy again.

interpretation.title: Mission after disappointment
interpretation.text: A historicist application may relate the sweet and bitter experience to a movement’s hopes and disappointment. The direct narrative is John’s experience and renewed commission. Any proposed later fulfilment must be presented as interpretation, not a name or date given here.

reflection: How could a disappointment prepare you to serve more thoughtfully?
prayer: Lord, help me receive Your word honestly and continue serving through disappointment. Amen.

heading: God’s witness will not be silenced.
time: The measuring and witness scenes continue the pause in the trumpet sequence. The seventh trumpet then looks ahead to God’s reign and final judgment.

scenes.title: Measuring the temple
scenes.text: John measures the temple, altar and worshippers. The outer court is excluded, and the holy city is trampled for forty-two months. The scene distinguishes what is measured from what is exposed.

scenes.title: Two witnesses testify
scenes.text: Two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth for 1,260 days. Their imagery recalls olive trees, lampstands, Elijah and Moses. Their authority comes from God.

scenes.title: Witnesses rejected
scenes.text: The beast from the bottomless pit kills the witnesses when their testimony is finished. Their enemies celebrate, exposing their hostility to the message.

scenes.title: God restores His witnesses
scenes.text: After three and a half days, God gives them life and calls them upward. Fear and an earthquake overturn the celebration. Their apparent defeat is not the last word.

scenes.title: The seventh trumpet
scenes.text: Heaven announces the kingdom of God and His Christ. Judgment, reward and the destruction of those who destroy the earth come into view. God’s temple opens, revealing the ark of His covenant.

symbols.title: Olive trees and lampstands
symbols.text: Zechariah’s vision links these pictures with God’s Spirit and His appointed servants.

symbols.title: Sodom and Egypt
symbols.text: Verse 8 says these names are used spiritually. They evoke rebellion and oppression rather than requiring one literal location for every detail.

symbols.title: Ark of the covenant
symbols.text: The ark recalls God’s covenant and the tablets kept with it, bringing faithfulness and judgment into view.

connections.title: Elijah’s witness
connections.text: Shutting heaven so that rain does not fall recalls Elijah’s prophetic ministry.

connections.title: Moses and the plagues
connections.text: Water turning to blood recalls the confrontation with Pharaoh.

questions.question: How long do the witnesses prophesy in sackcloth?
questions.answer: The stated period is 1,260 days.

questions.question: Who restores them to life?
questions.answer: The spirit of life from God enters them.

questions.question: What does the seventh trumpet announce?
questions.answer: The world’s kingdom belongs to the Lord and His Christ, who will reign for ever.

interpretation.title: The two witnesses in a historicist reading
interpretation.text: A traditional Adventist interpretation sees the Old and New Testaments represented by the witnesses. The chapter calls them God’s witnesses and uses prophetic imagery; it does not explicitly name the two Testaments. Read that identification as an interpretive application.

reflection: How can you remain a faithful witness when your beliefs are unpopular?
prayer: God, give me courage to speak truth with humility and love. Amen.

heading: The conflict behind the conflict.
time: This vision looks back to the Messiah’s birth and exaltation, reveals conflict in heaven, and follows opposition to God’s people. It is not simply an event after chapter 11.

scenes.title: The woman, child and dragon
scenes.text: A radiant woman gives birth while a dragon seeks to destroy her child. The child is caught up to God and His throne, and the woman finds a prepared place in the wilderness.

scenes.title: The accuser is cast down
scenes.text: Michael and his angels oppose the dragon. The text identifies the dragon as the devil and Satan. Heaven celebrates salvation, Christ’s authority and victory through the Lamb’s blood.

scenes.title: The woman is pursued
scenes.text: The dragon persecutes the woman. Wings, wilderness refuge and the earth swallowing a flood picture help amid danger.

scenes.title: The conflict continues
scenes.text: The dragon turns against the rest of the woman’s offspring, described as keeping God’s commandments and holding the testimony of Jesus Christ.

symbols.title: Dragon
symbols.text: The great dragon is the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, who deceives the world.

symbols.title: The male child
symbols.text: The ruler with a rod of iron recalls Psalm 2. Christians understand the child’s destiny and exaltation as pointing to Jesus the Messiah.

symbols.title: The woman
symbols.text: The woman represents God’s covenant people in this reading: the Messiah comes through Israel, and the vision continues with His faithful people.

connections.title: The serpent’s opposition
connections.text: Genesis introduces conflict between the serpent and the woman’s offspring.

connections.title: Carried on wings
connections.text: God’s care for Israel is described as carrying His people on eagles’ wings.

questions.question: Does the text identify the dragon?
questions.answer: Yes: the devil and Satan.

questions.question: How do the faithful overcome the accuser?
questions.answer: Through the Lamb’s blood and their testimony, remaining faithful even when life is threatened.

questions.question: How are the remaining offspring described?
questions.answer: They keep God’s commandments and have the testimony of Jesus Christ.

interpretation.title: A long conflict, not a label for our neighbours
interpretation.text: Historicist readers connect the wilderness period with prolonged persecution of the church. Identifying historical fulfilments is interpretation. The chapter’s named enemy is Satan; it does not license hatred toward people who believe differently.

reflection: What helps you remain faithful without treating other people as enemies?
prayer: Jesus, keep me close to You and make my witness courageous and kind. Amen.

heading: Who deserves your allegiance?
time: The vision develops the dragon’s opposition through two beasts. It revisits the struggle over worship and points toward a final crisis of coercion.

scenes.title: The beast from the sea
scenes.text: A beast combines features of a leopard, bear and lion. The dragon gives it power. A healed wound draws the world’s admiration, and worship is directed to the beast and dragon.

scenes.title: Power used against the saints
scenes.text: The beast speaks blasphemies and persecutes God’s people for forty-two months. The passage calls for patience and faith rather than admiration of force.

scenes.title: The beast from the earth
scenes.text: A second beast looks lamb-like but speaks as a dragon. Through signs and coercion it promotes worship of the first beast and an image made to it.

scenes.title: The mark and the number
scenes.text: Economic pressure is used to enforce allegiance. John calls for wisdom concerning the beast’s number, 666. The chapter presents a worship crisis, not a reason to fear every ordinary number or purchase.

symbols.title: Composite sea beast
symbols.text: Its animal features recall Daniel’s beasts, which are explained as kings or kingdoms. Revelation combines that language in a power opposed to God.

symbols.title: Lamb-like horns, dragon-like speech
symbols.text: The contrast suggests an appearance of gentleness joined to coercive behaviour. Judge the power by what it does.

symbols.title: Mark on hand or forehead
symbols.text: The mark signifies allegiance in the context of enforced worship and economic exclusion. Chapter 14 contrasts it with belonging to the Lamb.

connections.title: Worship under threat
connections.text: Daniel’s friends also face punishment for refusing to worship an image.

connections.title: God’s word and allegiance
connections.text: Commands bound to hand and forehead in Deuteronomy provide background for the language of loyalty.

questions.question: Who gives the first beast its authority?
questions.answer: The dragon.

questions.question: What reveals the second beast’s true character?
questions.answer: It speaks like a dragon and enforces worship through deception and threats.

questions.question: What qualities are urged upon the saints?
questions.answer: Patience and faith.

interpretation.title: Understanding the two beasts
interpretation.text: Adventist interpretation commonly identifies the sea beast with papal religious-political power and the earth beast with the United States in a future coercive role. These are historical and theological interpretations, not names printed in this chapter. They concern systems and actions, not the worth or sincerity of individual Catholics or Americans. This study does not identify a present-day purchase or technology as the mark.

reflection: How can you honour conscience when others disagree with you?
prayer: Lord, guard my loyalty to You and help me reject coercion in matters of faith. Amen.

heading: Good news and a serious choice.
time: The chapter contrasts the Lamb’s people with beast worship, then carries the vision forward to earth’s harvest. Its warnings follow the everlasting gospel.

scenes.title: With the Lamb
scenes.text: The 144,000 stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion. Their description stresses belonging, truthfulness and faithful devotion. The imagery should be read with the book’s wider contrast between pure and corrupt worship.

scenes.title: The first angel
scenes.text: The everlasting gospel goes to every nation, language and people. All are called to honour God and worship the Creator because the hour of His judgment has come.

scenes.title: Two further messages
scenes.text: Babylon’s fall is announced, followed by a warning against worshipping the beast and receiving its mark. The saints are described by endurance, God’s commandments and faith in Jesus. Those who die in the Lord are blessed.

scenes.title: The harvest
scenes.text: One like the Son of man appears on a cloud. Grain and grape harvests picture the completion of earth’s story and divine judgment. The severe winepress image is visionary, not an instruction for human violence.

symbols.title: Name on the forehead
symbols.text: This marks belonging to God and contrasts with the beast’s mark.

symbols.title: Babylon’s wine
symbols.text: Wine pictures the intoxicating influence of corrupt worship and unfaithfulness. Later chapters explain Babylon further.

symbols.title: Harvest
symbols.text: Harvest is used elsewhere for the completion of the age and the separation involved in judgment.

connections.title: Worship the Creator
connections.text: The wording recalls the creation language in the Sabbath commandment.

connections.title: The Son of man on clouds
connections.text: Daniel’s vision helps identify the royal significance of the figure on the cloud.

questions.question: Who is to hear the everlasting gospel?
questions.answer: Every nation, kindred, language and people.

questions.question: How are the saints described?
questions.answer: As keeping God’s commandments and the faith of Jesus, with patient endurance.

questions.question: What hope is given to those who die in the Lord?
questions.answer: They are blessed and rest from their labours; their works follow them.

interpretation.title: The three angels in Adventist mission
interpretation.text: Adventists understand these messages as a worldwide call to the gospel, Creator worship and faithfulness before Christ returns. The first message supplies the context for the warnings: salvation is announced before the call to choose. Historical applications should not replace that good news.

reflection: How can you share both the hope and seriousness of this message with kindness?
prayer: Creator and Redeemer, deepen my faith and help me share Your good news. Amen.

heading: A song of deliverance.
time: This short chapter introduces the seven last plagues. It first shows the victorious praising God, giving a glimpse of deliverance before the judgments are described.

scenes.title: The final plagues introduced
scenes.text: John sees seven angels with seven last plagues. They bring God’s wrath to its completion in this vision sequence.

scenes.title: The song of Moses and the Lamb
scenes.text: Those victorious over the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire. Their song praises God’s works, justice and holiness; it gives Him the honour for deliverance.

scenes.title: The sanctuary opened
scenes.text: Angels emerge from the heavenly temple and receive bowls of wrath. The temple fills with smoke from God’s glory and power. No one enters until the plagues are completed.

symbols.title: Song of Moses and the Lamb
symbols.text: The title joins the memory of deliverance from Egypt with salvation through Christ.

symbols.title: Sea of glass with fire
symbols.text: This recalls the throne-room sea in chapter 4, now seen with fire. The text does not explain every feature, so a detailed identification remains uncertain.

symbols.title: Smoke filling the temple
symbols.text: Earlier sanctuary scenes describe God’s glory filling a holy place and preventing entry.

connections.title: All nations worship
connections.text: The song echoes the hope that all nations will acknowledge God.

connections.title: Victory over the beast
connections.text: The singers’ victory answers the pressure to worship described in chapter 13.

questions.question: How are the seven plagues described?
questions.answer: As the last plagues, completing God’s wrath in this sequence.

questions.question: Who sings beside the sea?
questions.answer: Those who have gained victory over the beast, its image and the number of its name.

questions.question: What does their song say about God’s ways?
questions.answer: They are just and true.

interpretation.title: Judgment held within the story of salvation
interpretation.text: In the Adventist reading, these final plagues belong to the closing crisis before Christ’s return. The chapter itself introduces them as the last plagues. Begin with the song: the vision praises God’s justice rather than celebrating personal revenge.

reflection: What deliverance can you thank God for today?
prayer: God, teach me to trust Your justice and give You the praise for salvation. Amen.

heading: Evil’s rule reaches its limit.
time: The seven bowls describe the last plagues introduced in chapter 15. Within the chapter, the warning that Christ comes like a thief calls readers to remain ready.

scenes.title: The first three bowls
scenes.text: Sores afflict the beast’s worshippers; sea and fresh water become blood. Heavenly voices affirm God’s justice, connecting the judgments with the shedding of His people’s blood.

scenes.title: The fourth and fifth bowls
scenes.text: Scorching heat is followed by darkness over the beast’s kingdom. Those suffering blaspheme rather than repent. The narrative exposes entrenched resistance to God.

scenes.title: The sixth bowl
scenes.text: The Euphrates dries up. Three unclean spirits deceive the kings of the earth and gather them for the great day. A call to watchfulness interrupts the scene before the place is named Armageddon.

scenes.title: The seventh bowl
scenes.text: A voice declares completion. An unparalleled earthquake, Babylon’s judgment and great hail bring the vision to its climax. These are scenes of divine judgment, not a mandate for believers to harm others.

symbols.title: Frog-like spirits
symbols.text: They are spirits of devils working signs and gathering earthly rulers.

symbols.title: Drying Euphrates
symbols.text: The river evokes ancient Babylon and the removal of its support. The precise end-time application is interpreted differently.

symbols.title: Armageddon
symbols.text: It names the gathering place in the vision. The text gives no instructions for calculating a modern battle date.

connections.title: Plagues and hard hearts
connections.text: Exodus also joins plagues with resistance to God and His deliverance of His people.

connections.title: Watchfulness
connections.text: Jesus’ teaching about unexpected arrival helps explain the warning within the sixth bowl.

questions.question: What response recurs after the plagues?
questions.answer: People blaspheme and refuse to repent.

questions.question: What gathers the kings?
questions.answer: Deceptive spirits performing signs.

questions.question: What is the personal appeal in verse 15?
questions.answer: Stay watchful and keep your garments, an image of readiness.

interpretation.title: A worldwide conflict over worship
interpretation.text: Adventist interpretation reads Armageddon within the wider struggle over allegiance to God. Political headlines alone cannot explain the chapter: it explicitly names deceptive spirits and calls believers to watchfulness. It does not tell Christians to organise an earthly holy war.

reflection: How can you practise spiritual watchfulness without living in panic?
prayer: Lord, keep me alert to deception and steady in faith. Amen.

heading: Look beneath Babylon’s splendour.
time: An angel explains Babylon through a symbolic woman and beast. This expands the earlier announcements of Babylon’s fall rather than introducing an unrelated later city.

scenes.title: A glittering but violent power
scenes.text: John sees a richly dressed woman on a scarlet beast. Her golden cup hides corruption, and she is drunk with the blood of God’s witnesses. Outward splendour conceals spiritual unfaithfulness and persecution.

scenes.title: The beast explained
scenes.text: The angel describes heads, kings and horns. Their authority opposes the Lamb, but the Lamb overcomes because He is Lord of lords and King of kings.

scenes.title: The alliance breaks apart
scenes.text: The waters are explained as peoples and nations. The beast and horns turn against the woman. The powers that supported her become instruments of her ruin.

symbols.title: Many waters
symbols.text: The waters are peoples, multitudes, nations and languages.

symbols.title: Ten horns
symbols.text: They represent ten kings who share authority with the beast for a short period.

symbols.title: The woman
symbols.text: Verse 18 calls her the great city reigning over the kings of the earth. Understanding her wider religious significance involves interpretation.

connections.title: The ancient serpent · From Eden to Revelation
connections.text: Genesis 3 describes the serpent deceiving Eve and turning her away from God’s word. Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 identify the ancient serpent as the Devil and Satan, connecting the deceiver in Eden with the enemy who deceives the world. Revelation 13:2 then shows the dragon giving the beast its power and authority. The dragon and beast are connected, but they are distinct figures. This study’s application to papal religious-political power rests on its reading of those passages, not on a building’s appearance.

connections.title: Babylon by many waters
connections.text: Jeremiah’s description of Babylon supplies background for John’s language.

connections.title: A kingdom beyond earthly kings
connections.text: Daniel also pictures rulers opposing God before His kingdom prevails.

questions.question: Who explains the waters?
questions.answer: The angel: they represent peoples and nations.

questions.question: Why does the Lamb overcome?
questions.answer: He is Lord of lords and King of kings.

questions.question: Is Babylon’s alliance secure?
questions.answer: No. The beast and horns eventually turn against the woman.

interpretation.title: A system of unfaithfulness
interpretation.text: Historicist readers see Babylon as a corrupt religious-political system, not merely an ancient place. Proposed identities of the seven kings differ. The chapter’s clear contrast is between coercive, unfaithful power and the victorious Lamb; it does not justify hostility toward ordinary members of a religious community.

reflection: How can you tell the difference between impressive appearance and faithful character?
prayer: Jesus, give me discernment and keep my allegiance with You. Amen.

heading: Come out of what destroys.
time: The vision develops Babylon’s fall announced earlier. Laments from rulers, merchants and sailors show the collapse from several viewpoints rather than separate dated events.

scenes.title: A call to come out
scenes.text: Babylon’s corruption is exposed. God calls His people to leave so they will not share her sins and plagues. Her claim to invulnerability is answered by sudden judgment.

scenes.title: Those who profited mourn
scenes.text: Kings, merchants and seafarers grieve at the loss of luxury and trade. The cargo list ends with human lives, exposing the human cost beneath the wealth.

scenes.title: The end of a violent city
scenes.text: Heaven is called to recognise God’s judgment. A stone thrown into the sea pictures Babylon’s final fall. Music, industry and celebration cease; deception and bloodshed are named as reasons.

symbols.title: Babylon
symbols.text: The city embodies organised corruption, false worship and oppressive luxury in this reading. The image reaches beyond a warning about wealth alone.

symbols.title: A millstone in the sea
symbols.text: The angel uses the sinking stone to show Babylon’s violent and final overthrow.

symbols.title: A queen who cannot suffer
symbols.text: Her boast pictures arrogant security. The following judgment exposes the emptiness of that confidence.

connections.title: Leave Babylon
connections.text: Jeremiah’s call to flee Babylon is echoed in the appeal to God’s people.

connections.title: A merchant city lamented
connections.text: Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre provides background for the trade, ships and mourning in this chapter.

questions.question: Why are God’s people called out?
questions.answer: So they do not participate in Babylon’s sins or receive her plagues.

questions.question: What disturbing item ends the merchants’ list?
questions.answer: Human bodies and souls: people treated as merchandise.

questions.question: What offences does the ending emphasise?
questions.answer: Deception and responsibility for bloodshed.

interpretation.title: God has people to call out
interpretation.text: The wording “my people” matters: the call reaches people whom God loves within Babylon. Historicist applications to religious systems should preserve this distinction and avoid treating every individual as knowingly corrupt.

reflection: Is there a habit or loyalty you need to leave because it harms your conscience or others?
prayer: God, help me recognise compromise and follow Your call with courage. Amen.

heading: The faithful and true King.
time: Heaven celebrates Babylon’s judgment, followed by the marriage supper and the victorious Rider. The scene brings Christ’s triumph into view before the millennium of chapter 20.

scenes.title: Heaven praises God’s justice
scenes.text: Heaven’s praise responds to the judgment of the corrupt power that shed the blood of God’s servants. Salvation, glory and power belong to God.

scenes.title: The marriage of the Lamb
scenes.text: The bride is ready and receives fine linen. John is told that those invited to the marriage supper are blessed. When he tries to worship the angel, he is corrected: worship God.

scenes.title: The Rider on the white horse
scenes.text: He is called Faithful and True and the Word of God. He judges righteously and bears the title King of kings and Lord of lords. His weapon is pictured as a sword from His mouth.

scenes.title: The powers opposing Him fall
scenes.text: The beast, false prophet and assembled kings are defeated. The stark judgment scene declares the end of their resistance, not a battle plan for Christ’s followers to carry out.

symbols.title: Fine linen
symbols.text: The text identifies the linen with the righteousness, or righteous deeds, of the saints; it is granted to the bride.

symbols.title: Sword from the mouth
symbols.text: The picture points to the power of the King’s word in judgment, as in the earlier vision of Jesus.

symbols.title: The Rider
symbols.text: His titles include the Word of God and King of kings. They identify the scene as Christ’s royal victory.

connections.title: A feast of salvation
connections.text: Isaiah’s feast and defeat of death illuminate the hope represented by the Lamb’s supper.

connections.title: The true object of worship
connections.text: The angel refuses worship. Heavenly messengers direct attention to God rather than themselves.

questions.question: Who alone should receive worship?
questions.answer: God. The angel explicitly refuses John’s worship.

questions.question: What is the Rider called?
questions.answer: Faithful and True, the Word of God, and King of kings and Lord of lords.

questions.question: Who is blessed in the marriage scene?
questions.answer: Those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

interpretation.title: Receive the vision as a promise of victory
interpretation.text: Adventist readers understand the Rider’s triumph as Christ’s return and defeat of opposing powers. The images are visionary: the mouth-sword is not an instruction for human warfare. The focus is the faithful King whose authority ends evil’s rule.

reflection: What difference does trusting a faithful King make when human leaders disappoint you?
prayer: Jesus, prepare me to welcome You and live faithfully while I wait. Amen.

heading: Death will not have the last word.
time: The chapter describes a thousand-year period, then Satan’s final revolt and judgment. “Millennium” is simply a name for this thousand years.

scenes.title: Satan restrained
scenes.text: An angel binds Satan and confines him in the abyss so that he cannot deceive the nations until the thousand years are finished. His release afterward is brief.

scenes.title: The first resurrection
scenes.text: John sees judgment entrusted to those who reign with Christ. Those sharing in the first resurrection are blessed; the second death has no power over them.

scenes.title: The final deception fails
scenes.text: After the thousand years, Satan gathers the nations against the beloved city. Fire from God ends the assault. The devil’s opposition is finally judged.

scenes.title: Before the great white throne
scenes.text: The dead stand before God, and books are opened. Death and Hades surrender their dead and are cast into the lake of fire, called the second death. The book of life stands at the centre of the final distinction.

symbols.title: Chain and abyss
symbols.text: The vision pictures Satan’s restriction and inability to deceive during the thousand years. How this confinement is realised is an interpretive question.

symbols.title: Gog and Magog
symbols.text: Names from Ezekiel describe the nations in the final attack. Revelation explicitly gives the gathering a worldwide scope.

symbols.title: Lake of fire
symbols.text: Verse 14 calls it the second death. It includes the final disposal of death and Hades themselves.

connections.title: Books opened in judgment
connections.text: Daniel also sees a heavenly court with books opened and judgment in favour of the saints.

connections.title: Raised to meet the Lord
connections.text: Paul describes believers rising to meet Christ at His coming. Adventists read this together with the first resurrection.

questions.question: Why is Satan restrained?
questions.answer: So he cannot deceive the nations during the thousand years.

questions.question: What cannot harm those in the first resurrection?
questions.answer: The second death.

questions.question: Does death continue to rule forever?
questions.answer: No. Death and Hades are cast into the lake of fire.

interpretation.title: The Adventist understanding of the millennium
interpretation.text: Adventists understand the redeemed to be with Christ in heaven during the thousand years, with Satan confined to a desolated earth, followed by final judgment. That geographical synthesis draws on several passages; chapter 20 does not itself say “the saints spend the millennium in heaven.” Christians interpret these details differently.

reflection: How does the promise of final justice help you entrust unanswered questions to God?
prayer: God, help me trust Your just judgment and the life You offer in Christ. Amen.

heading: God makes His home with His people.
time: After final judgment, John sees a new heaven and new earth. The vision moves from the end of death to a detailed picture of the holy city.

scenes.title: All things made new
scenes.text: The holy city descends from God. He dwells with His people and removes tears, death, sorrow and pain. The promise comes with both an invitation to life and a warning against persistent evil.

scenes.title: The bride shown as a city
scenes.text: An angel shows John the New Jerusalem, radiant with God’s glory. Its gates carry the tribes’ names and its foundations the apostles’ names, joining the story of God’s people.

scenes.title: A city of beauty and fullness
scenes.text: The city is measured and described with gold, jewels and pearl gates. The extraordinary dimensions communicate the greatness of the promised home.

scenes.title: God and the Lamb are its light
scenes.text: There is no separate temple: God and the Lamb are its temple. Their glory lights the city. Nothing defiling enters; its inhabitants belong to the Lamb’s book of life.

symbols.title: Bride, the Lamb’s wife
symbols.text: The angel promises to show the bride and then shows the holy city. The city pictures the home and life of God’s covenant people.

symbols.title: Equal length, width and height
symbols.text: The cube-like dimensions recall the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple. This suggests a whole dwelling characterised by God’s presence.

symbols.title: Light without night
symbols.text: God’s glory illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its light.

connections.title: New heavens and a new earth
connections.text: Isaiah anticipates renewal and joy, language Revelation takes up in its final vision.

connections.title: God dwelling among His people
connections.text: The covenant promise of God’s presence reaches a fuller expression here.

questions.question: What happens to tears and death?
questions.answer: God wipes away tears, and death is no more.

questions.question: Why is there no temple building in the city?
questions.answer: God and the Lamb are its temple.

questions.question: Who gives the city its light?
questions.answer: God’s glory and the Lamb.

interpretation.title: Restoration is the destination
interpretation.text: The Adventist hope is a real renewed earth where God dwells with His redeemed people. The city’s visionary descriptions should lead us toward its explicit promises: no death, no pain and unhindered life with God. They are not permission to invent details the chapter does not supply.

reflection: Which promise in this chapter speaks most deeply to a loss you have experienced?
prayer: God, keep the hope of Your renewed world alive in me and make me a comfort to others. Amen.

heading: Come, Lord Jesus.
time: The restored creation scene continues, then the book returns to John and its readers with warnings, blessing and a final invitation. The closing dialogue is not a new event after eternity begins.

scenes.title: Life fully restored
scenes.text: A river flows from the throne of God and the Lamb. The tree of life bears fruit, the curse is gone, and God’s servants see His face. They live in His light and reign for ever.

scenes.title: These words are trustworthy
scenes.text: The angel affirms the message. John again must be redirected from worshipping the messenger. Unlike a sealed message reserved for later, this prophecy is to remain open for its readers.

scenes.title: An invitation to come
scenes.text: Jesus promises His coming and identifies Himself as the beginning and end, David’s root and offspring, and the bright morning star. The Spirit and the bride invite the thirsty to receive the water of life freely.

scenes.title: Keep the message faithfully
scenes.text: A solemn warning forbids adding to or taking from the prophecy. The book ends with a prayer for Jesus’ coming and a blessing of grace.

symbols.title: River of life
symbols.text: Ezekiel also sees life-giving water flowing from God’s dwelling. Here its source is the throne of God and the Lamb.

symbols.title: Tree of life
symbols.text: The tree returns from the Eden story. Access to life is restored, and the curse is removed.

symbols.title: Morning star
symbols.text: Jesus applies this title to Himself, completing the promise of the morning star in the letters.

connections.title: Water offered freely
connections.text: Isaiah’s invitation to the thirsty helps us hear the generosity of the final gospel invitation.

connections.title: Seeing God’s face
connections.text: The hope of seeing God is fulfilled in the servants’ unhindered fellowship with Him.

questions.question: What is absent from the restored creation?
questions.answer: The curse and night; God gives His servants light.

questions.question: Who may receive the water of life?
questions.answer: Anyone who thirsts and desires it is invited to take it freely.

questions.question: What prayer closes the book’s promise?
questions.answer: “Even so, come, Lord Jesus.”

interpretation.title: Hope without date-setting
interpretation.text: The promise of Christ’s coming calls for readiness, faithfulness and invitation. It does not provide a calendar date. A historicist study should end where the book ends: with Jesus, freely offered life and grace for those who hear.

reflection: What is one way you can live out Revelation’s hope and invitation this week?
prayer: Come, Lord Jesus. Until then, help me live by Your grace and invite others to Your life. Amen.
